sections.heading: Title
sections.text: From the University of Tokyo, NeurIPS 2022: the Langevin autoencoder. Langevin dynamics samples the intractable posteriors of deep latent models, but slowly. The authors amortize it into a shared encoder, prove it valid MCMC, and beat variational autoencoders.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.text: Training deep latent variable models by maximum likelihood needs an expectation over the latent posterior, which is intractable. Langevin dynamics samples that posterior accurately, but runs a fresh chain per data point and converges slowly.

sections.heading: Motivation
sections.text: Variational inference dominates thanks to amortization: one shared encoder predicts the latents for all data. But it relies on tractable Gaussians, limiting accuracy. MCMC has no such limit, yet nobody truly amortized it before. The goal: amortized efficiency with MCMC flexibility.

sections.heading: Contribution
sections.text: Two contributions. First, amortized Langevin dynamics: an MCMC algorithm that replaces per-datapoint iterations with Langevin updates on a shared encoder's parameters, proven valid. Second, the Langevin autoencoder, a generative model that is a small tweak of a standard autoencoder.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: The key idea: move randomness from latent space to encoder parameters. A deterministic encoder maps observations to latents; updating its parameters moves the samples. Convergence is guaranteed when a fixed feature extractor feeds a linear layer wider than the batch. The autoencoder runs a few steps before each decoder update, optionally with Metropolis-Hastings.

sections.heading: Dataset / Benchmark
sections.text: Validation comes in two stages. First, toy problems with known answers: a bivariate-Gaussian posterior and a random-network posterior. Then image generation on MNIST, S-V-H-N, CIFAR-10, and CelebA, scored by negative ELBO per dimension over three seeds.

sections.heading: Key Result
sections.text: On toy problems, amortized Langevin dynamics reproduces multimodal, correlated posteriors that variational inference misses. On images, the Langevin autoencoder achieves the lowest negative ELBO on all four datasets. The lesson: more accurate posterior sampling yields better models.

sections.heading: Ablation Study
sections.text: Two ablations. Encoder capacity confirms the theory: when the final linear layer is at least the batch size, samples match; smaller, some collapse. On images, the Metropolis-Hastings step stabilizes training, while iteration count barely matters beyond two.

sections.heading: Headline Numbers
sections.text: The gains are consistent but modest. On MNIST, negative ELBO drops to one point one seven seven, versus one point one eight nine for the VAE. CIFAR-10, CelebA, and S-V-H-N show similar small improvements. The cost: about two-and-a-quarter times slower than a VAE.

sections.heading: Takeaway
sections.text: The takeaway is elegant: move Langevin noise from the latents to the encoder's parameters, so sampling becomes both efficient and flexible. Provably valid, it looks almost like a standard autoencoder yet consistently beats variational autoencoders on test likelihood.
